source_span: More demand + lower prices is not automatically bullish if pricing falls faster than consumption grows. Unless capability keeps making radical jumps (looking at you, Astra)… periods of compute oversupply become plausible.
source_chain: Token prices are collapsing faster than usage can offset (Silicon Data token index -29% in August) therefore per-token pricing looks like a phase, not a durable model, so more demand at falling prices does not equal bullish equities therefore the AI complex de-rates and credit reprices even though demand/capability is real; invalidation: unless a radical capability jump (Astra) breaks the pattern, compute oversupply is plausible.
pulse_chain: Broadcom beats and guides AI revenue to double to $115bn then $230bn, but the stock falls on a Q4 miss versus Goldman's number, and one soft quarter is not why a two-year doubling gets sold therefore the real sell is the token price collapse (Silicon Data index -29% to $0.97/M, >50% off May's $2.05 peak) with volume up ~47% (JPMorgan) but dollar spend only ~7%, set against ~$737bn hyperscaler capex (38% of revenue) and 78/91 2026 hyperscaler bonds trading below issue therefore demand can be enormous and stocks still fall if it arrives at a price that doesn't service the debt raised to build capacity; invalidation: absent a capability jump like Astra (Critical cybersecurity threshold cleared Sept 1, no confirmed launch date), compute oversupply stays plausible.
why: The pulse carries Privorotsky's exact mechanism (price collapse outrunning volume growth makes demand non-bullish), the same capex/credit consequence, and the identical Astra invalidation, correctly attributed to Goldman, with JPMorgan's volume/spend split correctly sourced separately.
